content: I am planning a vegetable garden for the first time. Where should I start?

A good place to start is a small bed, about two metres by one, in a spot that gets six to eight hours of direct sun a day. Small beds are easy to weed and water, and mistakes cost little. Before planting, loosen the soil to the depth of a spade and mix in a few centimetres of compost, since most vegetables grow best in loose, rich soil that drains well. For a first year, choose crops that forgive beginners: lettuce, radishes, bush beans and courgettes all grow quickly and give a harvest within a couple of months.
How often should I water them?

Water deeply rather than often. A thorough soaking two or three times a week encourages roots to grow downward, which makes the plants more resistant to dry spells, while a light sprinkle every day keeps the roots near the surface. Push a finger into the soil up to the second knuckle: if it feels dry there, it is time to water. Early morning is the best time, because the leaves dry quickly in the sun and the plants have moisture to draw on through the hottest part of the day.

The most common mistakes are planting too much at once, crowding the seedlings and overwatering. Read the spacing on the seed packet and thin the seedlings as they come up, even though it feels wasteful, because crowded plants compete for light and are more likely to get disease. Keep a notebook of what you planted and when, and what went well, so that next season you can build on it. Above all, expect a few failures; every gardener has them, and they teach more than the successes.
